title: Attention Is All You Need
content: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
Google Brain; Google Research; University of Toronto; Independent (work performed while at Google Research)
31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2017)
A new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.
presenter_notes: Good morning/afternoon. Today, I'll present a paper that introduced a fundamental shift in how we model sequences, proving that attention mechanisms are all you need.

title: Background: Sequence Transduction is Fundamental
content: Tasks like machine translation, text summarization, and speech recognition are core to NLP.
The dominant approach for over a decade: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs).
RNNs process sequences step-by-step, maintaining a hidden state that encodes history.
The encoder-decoder framework became standard: an encoder reads the input, a decoder generates the output.
Attention mechanisms were later added, allowing the decoder to focus on relevant parts of the input sequence.
presenter_notes: Sequence transduction is everywhere. For years, RNNs were the go-to architecture. They work well but have a fundamental bottleneck we'll discuss next.

title: The Problem: The Sequential Computation Bottleneck
content: RNNs are inherently sequential: to process position 'n', you must first process positions 1 through n-1.
This results in O(n) sequential operations, severely limiting parallelization during training.
Long training times for long sequences become a major practical constraint.
Convolutional approaches (ByteNet, ConvS2S) enable parallel computation but introduce another issue...
The number of operations needed to connect distant positions grows with the distance (e.g., O(log_k(n))), making long-range dependencies harder to learn.

presenter_notes: RNNs are slow due to sequential dependency. CNNs are parallel but struggle with long-range connections. We need a model that is both highly parallel and can directly connect any two words.

title: Our Solution: The Transformer
content: Core Idea: Rely solely on attention mechanisms to compute representations. No recurrence, no convolution.
Maintains the proven encoder-decoder structure, but both are stacks of identical layers.
Each layer has two sub-layers: Multi-Head Self-Attention and a Position-wise Feed-Forward Network.
Residual connections and layer normalization are used around each sub-layer.
To inject sequence order, we add Positional Encodings to the input embeddings.
presenter_notes: We propose the Transformer. Its key innovation is using attention for everything. This architecture is designed for maximum parallelization and direct modeling of all pairwise relationships.

title: Technical Core: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
content: Attention is a function that maps a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output.
The output is a weighted sum of the values, where the weight is the compatibility of the query with each key.
We compute this for a matrix of queries Q, keys K, and values V simultaneously.

equation_reference.context: In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V . We compute the matrix of outputs as: Attention(Q, K, V ) = softmax(QKT √ dk )V (1) The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multi- plicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of √ 1 dk . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

presenter_notes: The core operation is scaled dot-product attention. We compute similarity (dot product) between queries and keys, scale it to stabilize gradients, apply softmax to get weights, and use these to weight the values.

title: Technical Core: Multi-Head Attention
content: Single attention head performs a weighted average, which can be limiting.
Multi-Head Attention runs 'h' attention heads in parallel, each with its own learned linear projections.
This allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces.
The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected to the final dimension.

figure_reference.caption: (left) Scaled Dot-Product Attention. (right) Multi-Head Attention consists of several attention layers running in parallel.

equation_reference.latex: MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h)W^O \\ where \ head_i = Attention(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)
equation_reference.context: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this. MultiHead(Q, K, V ) = Concat(head1, ..., headh)WO where headi = Attention(QWQ i , KW K i , V WV i ) Where the projections are parameter matrices W Q i ∈ R dmodel×dk , W K i ∈ R dmodel×dk , WV i ∈ R dmodel×dv and WO ∈ R hdv×dmodel .

presenter_notes: Multi-head attention is like having multiple sets of eyes, each looking for different types of relationships—one for syntax, one for semantics, one for coreference, etc.

title: Model Details: Positional Encoding & Feed-Forward Network
content: Since the model has no recurrence or convolution, we must explicitly inject information about the order of the sequence.
We use sinusoidal positional encodings added to the input embeddings.
These encodings allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions and generalize to longer sequences.
Each layer also contains a Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN): a simple two-layer MLP with ReLU, applied identically to each position.

equation_reference.context: In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies: P E(pos,2i) = sin(pos/100002i/dmodel) P E(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/100002i/dmodel) where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π. We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos.

presenter_notes: We need to tell the model about word order. Sinusoidal encodings are a clever, fixed pattern that works well. The FFN adds non-linearity and processing power to each position independently.

title: Experimental Setup
content: Tasks: Machine Translation on two major benchmarks.
WMT 2014 English-to-German (EN-DE): 4.5M sentence pairs.
WMT 2014 English-to-French (EN-FR): 36M sentence pairs.
Evaluation Metric: BLEU score.
Baselines: State-of-the-art models including GNMT+RL, ConvS2S, and their ensembles.
Training: Adam optimizer with a novel learning rate schedule (warmup then decay).

equation_reference.context: We used the Adam optimizer [20] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98 and ϵ = 10−9 . We varied the learning rate over the course of training, according to the formula: lrate = d −0.5 model · min(step_num−0.5 , step_num · warmup_steps−1.5 ) (3) This corresponds to increasing the learning rate linearly for the first warmup_steps training steps, and decreasing it thereafter proportionally to the inverse square root of the step number. We used warmup_steps = 4000.

presenter_notes: We evaluated on standard translation tasks. We compare against the best models of the time and use a careful training schedule.

title: Key Result: New State-of-the-Art in Translation
content: The 'big' Transformer model sets new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU scores.
EN-DE: 28.4 BLEU, improving over the previous best (an ensemble) by over 2 BLEU.
EN-FR: 41.8 BLEU, a new single-model SOTA.
Crucially, these results were achieved with a fraction of the training cost (FLOPs).
For example, on EN-FR, Transformer big used ~1/50th the FLOPs of the best previous ensemble.

table_reference.caption: Table 2: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.

presenter_notes: The results are clear: Transformer achieves higher quality with dramatically lower training cost. It's not just a better model; it's a more efficient one.

title: Ablation Study: Validating Design Choices
content: We conducted extensive experiments to understand the impact of each component.
Key Findings:
1. 8 attention heads is optimal. Too few or too many hurts performance.
2. Reducing the key dimension (d_k) degrades quality, confirming the need for sufficient dimensionality in the dot-product.
3. Larger models (more layers, larger dimensions) perform better, as expected.
4. Dropout is crucial for preventing overfitting.
5. Sinusoidal and learned positional encodings perform nearly identically.

table_reference.caption: Table 3: Variations on the Transformer architecture. Unlisted values are identical to those of the base model. All metrics are on the English-to-German translation development set, newstest2013. Listed perplexities are per-wordpiece, according to our byte-pair encoding, and should not be compared to per-word perplexities.

presenter_notes: This table shows our design choices are well-founded. The model is robust, and components like multi-head attention and dropout are essential.

title: Interpretability: What Do the Attention Heads Learn?
content: Multi-head attention is not just effective; it's also interpretable.
Different heads learn to perform different, often linguistically plausible, tasks.
Example 1: Capturing long-range syntactic dependencies (e.g., verb 'making' to 'difficult').
Example 2: Performing anaphora resolution (e.g., pronoun 'its' to antecedents 'Law' and 'application').
Example 3: Attending to immediate neighbors or sentence boundaries, capturing structural patterns.

figure_reference.caption: An example of the attention mechanism following long-distance dependencies in the encoder self-attention in layer 5 of 6. Many of the attention heads attend to a distant dependency of the verb 'making', completing the phrase 'making...more difficult'. Attentions here shown only for the word 'making'. Different colors represent different heads. Best viewed in color.

presenter_notes: The model isn't a black box. We can visualize attention patterns and see heads specializing in tasks like linking verbs to their modifiers or resolving pronouns.

title: Interpretability: Specialized Attention Heads
content: Further evidence of head specialization from the same encoder layer.
One head attends strongly to the immediate next word (learning local bigram patterns).
Another head attends broadly to the end of the sentence (perhaps capturing sentential scope or global structure).
This demonstrates the 'multi-head' design works as intended: different representation subspaces capture different relationships.

figure_reference.caption: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution. Top: Full attentions for head 5. Bottom: Isolated attentions from just the word 'its' for attention heads 5 and 6. Note that the attentions are very sharp for this word.

presenter_notes: Here, we see heads resolving what 'its' refers to. Head 5 focuses on 'Law', head 6 on 'application'. The model learns to decompose the task of coreference.

title: Generalization: Strong Performance on Parsing
content: To test if the Transformer is a general-purpose architecture, we applied it to English constituency parsing.
Task: Predict the syntactic tree structure of a sentence.
With only 40K training sentences (WSJ only), a 4-layer Transformer achieved 91.3 F1, outperforming strong discriminative parsers like the Berkeley Parser (90.4).
In a semi-supervised setting with more data, it achieved 92.7 F1, showing competitive performance.
This proves the Transformer's versatility beyond machine translation.

title: Conclusion & Core Contributions
content: The Transformer introduced a paradigm shift: attention mechanisms alone are sufficient for state-of-the-art sequence modeling.
Key Contributions:
1. **Architecture**: A novel, recurrence-free, convolution-free encoder-decoder model based solely on attention.
2. **Efficiency**: Massively parallelizable, leading to drastically reduced training times.
3. **Modeling**: Constant operational path length between any two positions, facilitating learning of long-range dependencies.
4. **Performance**: Achieved new SOTA results on major machine translation benchmarks with lower cost.
5. **Generality**: Demonstrated strong performance on English constituency parsing.
presenter_notes: In summary, the Transformer proved that attention is all you need. It solved the parallelization problem of RNNs and the long-range dependency problem of CNNs, setting a new foundation for NLP.

title: Impact & Future Directions
content: Impact: The Transformer has become the foundational architecture for nearly all modern NLP (BERT, GPT, T5, etc.).
Future Directions (as envisioned in the paper):
1. Extending attention to other modalities (images, audio, video).
2. Investigating efficient (local/restricted) attention for very long sequences.
3. Exploring non-autoregressive or less sequential generation methods.
The paper's final sentence: 'We leave this for future work.'
presenter_notes: This work didn't just propose a model; it defined a new paradigm. Its impact is immense, powering the LLM revolution. The future directions it outlined are still active areas of research today.
